title: The Peace Table
theme: Mediation, conflict resolution, and building bridges between opposing groups
description: Two school groups are at war. As mediator, you'll listen to both sides, uncover hidden motivations, deal with spoilers, and try to build a lasting peace. Over 10 rounds, you'll learn that most conflicts aren't about what they seem to be about.
learning_objectives: Learn to listen without taking sides in a conflict
Understand that most conflicts have hidden motivations beneath the surface
Practice building agreements that address real needs, not just stated positions
how_to_play: Each round reveals new information about the conflict. As mediator, your neutrality, trust from both sides, information, and patience all matter. One wrong move can collapse the entire process.

glossary_terms.definition: A process where a neutral person helps two sides find a solution together, without imposing one
Not favouring either side — listening equally to both perspectives
What someone actually wants beneath what they say they want — the real need behind the stated demand
A person who benefits from the conflict continuing and actively works to prevent resolution
Reducing the intensity of a conflict — lowering emotions so people can think clearly

rounds.title: Understanding Both Sides
rounds.situation: {player_name}, the principal has asked you to mediate between two groups. Group A: the 'Literary Club' (led by Shruti) claims the 'Science Club' (led by Arjun, Group B) took over their room, their notice board, and their budget. Group B says the Literary Club wasted their budget on useless events and the room was reassigned fairly by the teacher-in-charge. Both groups have stopped talking to each other. Some members are spreading rumours.
rounds.story: Before you can fix anything, you need to understand what actually happened — and what's really going on underneath.
rounds.image_prompt: Two groups of Indian students on opposite sides of a school corridor, arms crossed, student mediator in the middle looking calm
rounds.coaching_moment: The first step in any mediation is listening — not to respond, but to truly understand each side's experience.

choices.label: Meet both groups together first
choices.description: Bring everyone to one table. Let both sides state their case. Open and transparent.
choices.consequence_hint: Transparent, but emotions are too high — a joint meeting might turn into a shouting match

events.description: The meeting lasts 8 minutes before Shruti and Arjun start talking over each other. Three people walk out.

choices.label: Meet each group separately first
choices.description: Private meetings with each group. Listen without judging. Gather information before bringing them together.
choices.consequence_hint: Builds trust with each side, but they might wonder what you're telling the other group

events.description: Shruti tells you things she'd never say in front of Arjun. Arjun opens up about pressures you didn't expect.

choices.label: Read all the documents first
choices.description: Before meeting anyone, review the budget records, room allocation emails, and event reports. Let the facts speak.
choices.consequence_hint: Data-driven and neutral, but both groups might feel ignored while you read paperwork

events.description: The budget records tell an interesting story. The Literary Club spent 80% of their budget on one event. The room was reassigned without notice.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Private Meetings
rounds.situation: In your private meeting with Shruti, {player_name}, she breaks down: 'It's not about the room. Arjun told everyone our literary magazine was a waste of paper. My parents already say writing is useless. When even school doesn't value it...' In your meeting with Arjun, he says coldly: 'The Literary Club had three years to prove itself. Their last event had 12 attendees. Science Club events get 200. Resources should go where there's impact.'
rounds.story: Beneath the surface fight about rooms and budgets, there are deeper feelings — about validation, respect, and what's considered 'valuable.'
rounds.image_prompt: Indian girl student upset in a private meeting, then Indian boy student making a logical argument in separate meeting, mediator listening to both
rounds.coaching_moment: Most conflicts aren't about what people say they're about. A fight about a room is rarely just about a room.

choices.label: Validate both perspectives openly
choices.description: Tell Shruti her feelings are valid and tell Arjun his logic makes sense. Acknowledge what each side needs.
choices.consequence_hint: Both feel heard, but they might later feel you agreed with the other side too

events.description: Both groups tell their friends: 'At least the mediator listened.' Trust in the process increases.

choices.label: Challenge each side's blind spots
choices.description: Ask Shruti: 'Why did only 12 people attend?' Ask Arjun: 'Have you ever read the literary magazine?'
choices.consequence_hint: Pushes both sides to reflect, but they might feel attacked and lose trust in you

events.description: Shruti gets defensive. Arjun pauses. 'No, I haven't read it,' he admits quietly.

choices.label: Focus on shared interests
choices.description: Ask each side: 'What would an ideal outcome look like for you?' Find where their answers overlap.
choices.consequence_hint: Forward-looking and solution-oriented, but might skip the emotional processing both sides need

events.description: Both sides want 'respect for their work.' Neither cares about the room as much as they care about being taken seriously.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Discovering the Hidden Motivation
rounds.situation: {player_name}, during your investigation you discover something unexpected. The teacher-in-charge, Mrs. Iyer, reassigned the room because she personally dislikes the Literary Club advisor, Mr. Das. It was never about club performance. Mrs. Iyer and Mr. Das had a disagreement about teaching methods last year. The students are fighting a proxy war for a teacher conflict they don't even know about.
rounds.story: The real source of the conflict isn't between the students at all.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student mediator discovering documents showing teacher conflict, realization on face, school staff room visible
rounds.coaching_moment: Sometimes the visible conflict is just the surface — the real forces are hidden, and understanding them changes everything.

choices.label: Share the discovery with both groups
choices.description: Tell Shruti and Arjun what you found. They deserve to know the real reason behind the room reassignment.
choices.consequence_hint: Transparency shifts the blame away from students, but exposing teachers' politics could create a bigger mess

events.description: Both groups are stunned. Shruti says, 'So this was never about us?' Arjun looks angry. 'We've been fighting each other for nothing.'

choices.label: Raise it with the principal privately
choices.description: Tell the principal about the teacher conflict. Let them handle the adult issue while you focus on the student mediation.
choices.consequence_hint: Smart separation of issues, but the students' conflict won't fully resolve until the root cause is addressed

events.description: The principal is surprised and concerned. They say they'll look into it. Meanwhile, you continue the student mediation.

choices.label: Keep it to yourself for now
choices.description: Use the knowledge to guide the mediation without revealing the source. Steer both groups toward a solution that bypasses the teacher conflict.
choices.consequence_hint: You control the narrative, but you're withholding important information from people who deserve it

events.description: You guide the conversation carefully, avoiding the teacher topic. Both sides cooperate but don't understand why you seem so relaxed about the room.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Finding Common Ground
rounds.situation: {player_name}, after multiple meetings, you've identified one potential common ground: both clubs want to do a big event that showcases student talent. The Literary Club wants a literary festival. The Science Club wants a science exhibition. What if they did a joint 'Knowledge Festival' — combining both? Shruti is cautiously interested. Arjun says, 'Why should we share when we can do it better alone?'
rounds.story: The first real opportunity for collaboration is on the table. But one side is resistant.
rounds.image_prompt: Two Indian students sitting across table with a joint event proposal between them, mediator facilitating, cautious optimism
rounds.coaching_moment: Finding common ground doesn't mean both sides agree on everything — it means finding the one thing they care about equally.

choices.label: Pitch the joint event enthusiastically
choices.description: Present a detailed plan for the Knowledge Festival. Show how both clubs benefit — shared budget, shared audience, shared credit.
choices.consequence_hint: A concrete plan is persuasive, but if you push too hard, resistant members will dig in

events.description: Shruti agrees immediately. Arjun asks for time to think. Two Science Club members message you privately: 'We like the idea.'

choices.label: Let them discover it themselves
choices.description: Instead of proposing the joint event, ask both groups: 'What's the one event you'd love the whole school to attend?' Let the idea emerge naturally.
choices.consequence_hint: Takes longer but if they come up with it themselves, they'll own it more deeply

events.description: After 30 minutes of discussion, Ananya from the Science Club says, 'What if we did something together?' Shruti's eyes light up.

choices.label: Address Arjun's resistance first
choices.description: Before pushing the joint event, meet Arjun alone. Understand why he's resistant. There might be a deeper concern.
choices.consequence_hint: Shows you won't ignore resistance, but Shruti might feel you're spending too much time on the other side

events.description: Arjun admits: 'I'm worried they'll take credit for our work. Last time we collaborated, they presented our charts as theirs.'

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Dealing with Spoilers
rounds.situation: Just when things were improving, {player_name}, a senior student named Vikram — who isn't in either club — starts a WhatsApp group called 'Literary Club Exposed.' He posts old screenshots of club members mocking Science Club projects. The screenshots are real but taken out of context. Both groups are furious again. Vikram seems to enjoy the drama.
rounds.story: A spoiler has entered the process. Someone who benefits from the conflict continuing.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian senior student smirking at phone while two groups of upset students look at their phones, mediator looking concerned
rounds.coaching_moment: In every conflict, there are people who benefit from it continuing. Identifying the spoiler is as important as understanding the conflict itself.
rounds.timer_narrative: Both groups are threatening to pull out of the mediation...

choices.label: Expose Vikram's motives publicly
choices.description: In a joint meeting, reveal that Vikram isn't in either club, has no stake, and is stirring drama for entertainment. Name the spoiler.
choices.consequence_hint: Unites both groups against a common external threat, but you're making an enemy of Vikram

events.description: Both groups turn their anger toward Vikram. Shruti and Arjun share a look — the first time they've agreed on anything.

choices.label: Ignore Vikram, refocus the groups
choices.description: Don't give Vikram attention. Remind both groups that the screenshots are old and out of context. Redirect to the joint event planning.
choices.consequence_hint: Keeps the process on track, but Vikram continues stirring trouble in the background

events.description: Both groups calm down slowly. Vikram's group loses interest when no one engages. But some damage is done.

choices.label: Talk to Vikram directly
choices.description: Meet Vikram one-on-one. Find out why he's doing this. Maybe he can be neutralized or even brought into the process.
choices.consequence_hint: Understanding the spoiler might reveal useful information, but it takes time and energy away from the actual mediation

events.description: Vikram admits he was rejected from the Science Club last year. 'If they don't want me, why should they get nice things?' There's a hurt person underneath the troublemaker.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Joint Session — United Front
rounds.situation: After exposing Vikram, something unexpected happened, {player_name}. Shruti and Arjun started texting each other for the first time — bonding over shared annoyance at Vikram. They're ready for a joint meeting. This is the first time both groups will sit in the same room since the conflict started. The energy is cautious but not hostile.
rounds.story: A shared enemy created a window. Now you need to use it before it closes.
rounds.image_prompt: Two groups of Indian students sitting together at a table for the first time, cautious but hopeful, mediator facilitating
rounds.coaching_moment: A window of goodwill in mediation is fragile — you have to move quickly but carefully to build something lasting.
rounds.timer_narrative: Both groups are here but the goodwill won't last forever...

choices.label: Start with shared grievances
choices.description: Begin by having both groups share what frustrated them about the situation. Create empathy by showing they both felt similar things.
choices.consequence_hint: Powerful emotional connection, but reopening wounds risks reigniting the conflict

events.description: Arjun says, 'I felt disrespected when people said science is boring.' Shruti says, 'I felt invisible when our work was dismissed.' They look at each other. Something shifts.

choices.label: Go straight to the joint event plan
choices.description: Skip the emotional stuff. Use the momentum. Start planning the Knowledge Festival together — practical collaboration.
choices.consequence_hint: Productive and forward-looking, but unresolved emotions may surface later during the planning

events.description: They start dividing responsibilities. The Literary Club handles writing and presentations. Science Club handles experiments and displays. It works — for now.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Joint Session — Tense Start
rounds.situation: {player_name}, both groups have agreed to a joint meeting, but the atmosphere is tense. Vikram's WhatsApp group is still active and both sides are wary. Shruti says, 'I'll come, but if they disrespect us one more time, we're done.' Arjun says, 'We have nothing to apologize for.' You need to set the tone immediately.
rounds.story: The first joint session can make or break the entire mediation. The opening moments matter most.
rounds.image_prompt: Two groups of Indian students sitting on opposite sides of a table, arms crossed, mediator standing between them, tense atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: In mediation, the facilitator's energy sets the room's temperature. If you're calm, the room has a chance to be calm.
rounds.timer_narrative: People are getting up to leave...

choices.label: Set ground rules immediately
choices.description: 'Before anyone speaks: no interrupting, no personal attacks, no phones. You can disagree but with respect. Agreed?'
choices.consequence_hint: Structure creates safety, but some members might feel you're being controlling

events.description: Both groups nod reluctantly. The ground rules create a container. The first 10 minutes are tense but nobody shouts.

choices.label: Start with a surprising question
choices.description: 'Before we talk about the conflict — tell me one thing you actually respect about the other club.' Force them to see the other side's value.
choices.consequence_hint: If it works, it immediately changes the energy. If it falls flat, the silence will be painful.

events.description: Silence. Then a Science Club member says, 'Their magazine cover last year was actually really good.' A Literary Club member says, 'Your robotics demo was cool.' The ice cracks.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Breakthrough Moment
rounds.situation: Midway through the joint session, {player_name}, something unexpected happens. Shruti says to Arjun: 'I read your project on water purification. It was actually brilliant. Why didn't anyone tell us about it?' Arjun pauses. Then says: 'I read your poem in the magazine last year. It made me think. I never told you.' The room goes quiet.
rounds.story: Real breakthroughs in mediation happen when people see each other as human beings, not opponents.
rounds.image_prompt: Two Indian students making eye contact across a table with surprised, softened expressions, other students watching with emotion
rounds.coaching_moment: Conflict resolution happens when people stop seeing 'the other side' and start seeing people.
rounds.timer_narrative: The moment is fragile — what you do next matters enormously...

choices.label: Stay silent — let the moment breathe
choices.description: Don't say anything. Let Shruti and Arjun's words hang in the air. Sometimes the mediator's best tool is silence.
choices.consequence_hint: Powerful and respectful of the moment, but the silence might become awkward and the moment could pass

events.description: The silence lasts 10 seconds. It feels like forever. Then Shruti says, 'Maybe we should have talked to each other instead of about each other.' Arjun nods.

choices.label: Build on it immediately
choices.description: 'This is exactly what I was hoping for. You both create amazing things. Imagine what you could create together. Let's talk about the joint festival — right now.'
choices.consequence_hint: Channels the emotional energy into action, but might feel too transactional — like you used their vulnerability

events.description: Both groups start talking about the festival with real energy. Ideas flow. The mood shifts from conflict to creation.

choices.label: Ask everyone else to share
choices.description: 'Shruti and Arjun just shared something real. Does anyone else want to say something they've never told the other group?'
choices.consequence_hint: Opens the floodgates — could be beautiful or could get messy fast

events.description: Three more students share. One says something harsh. Another apologizes for a rumour they spread. The room is emotional but real.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Drafting the Agreement
rounds.situation: It's time to write it down, {player_name}. Both groups have agreed in principle to a joint Knowledge Festival and shared room usage. But the details matter: Who controls the budget? Whose name goes first on posters? What happens if one club feels the other isn't doing their share? Agreements fail in the details.
rounds.story: A handshake is good. A written agreement with clear terms is better.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian students writing an agreement document together at a table, mediator helping, pens and paper, collaborative atmosphere
rounds.coaching_moment: The strength of an agreement isn't in the words — it's in whether both sides feel the terms are fair enough to follow.
rounds.timer_narrative: Both groups want to finalize before school ends today...

choices.label: Write detailed terms together
choices.description: Go through every detail: budget split, responsibilities, timeline, dispute resolution, consequences for non-compliance.
choices.consequence_hint: Thorough and prevents future arguments, but the process is tedious and people's patience is running thin

events.description: The agreement is 2 pages. Both groups sign it. One person says, 'This feels like a contract.' Another says, 'That's the point.'

choices.label: Keep it simple — principles, not rules
choices.description: Write 5 simple principles: equal respect, shared credit, joint decision-making, open communication, fairness. Trust them to figure out the details.
choices.consequence_hint: Elegant and trusting, but vague principles can be interpreted differently by each side when disagreements arise

events.description: Both groups sign. The principles are pinned on the shared notice board. Simple, visible, and something to point to.

choices.label: Let them write it themselves
choices.description: Step back. Ask a member from each group to co-write the agreement. Your job as mediator is done — they need to own this.
choices.consequence_hint: Empowering, but they might struggle to agree on even the language without your facilitation

events.description: Shruti and a Science Club member spend an hour writing. They argue twice but resolve it themselves. The agreement has both their handwriting.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: The Implementation Challenge
rounds.situation: Two weeks into the agreement, {player_name}, problems surface. The Science Club says the Literary Club isn't contributing enough to event logistics. The Literary Club says the Science Club made poster decisions without consulting them. Both groups message you: 'The agreement isn't working.' Old tensions bubble up.
rounds.story: Every agreement faces its first test. This is the moment that determines if it was real or just words.
rounds.image_prompt: Two Indian students arguing over event posters, mediator receiving messages on phone, school event preparation in background
rounds.coaching_moment: Agreements don't fail because they're badly written — they fail because people stop talking when problems arise.
rounds.timer_narrative: The Knowledge Festival is in 10 days and preparation is stalling...

choices.label: Call an emergency mediation session
choices.description: Bring both groups back to the table. Address the specific issues. Amend the agreement if needed.
choices.consequence_hint: Responsive and proactive, but constant mediation creates dependency — they need to resolve things without you

events.description: The session is shorter this time. Issues are resolved in 40 minutes. But you wonder — will they call you every time?

choices.label: Tell them to solve it themselves
choices.description: 'You have an agreement. Use it. Talk to each other directly. I believe you can figure this out.'
choices.consequence_hint: Empowering if they rise to it, risky if they can't — the whole agreement could collapse

events.description: Shruti and Arjun have a tense phone call. Then a productive one. They resolve the poster issue. They didn't need you this time.

choices.label: Coach one side privately
choices.description: Meet the group that's struggling more and help them communicate their concerns clearly to the other group.
choices.consequence_hint: Helpful for the struggling group, but your neutrality takes a hit if the other side finds out

events.description: The coached group communicates clearly. The issue is resolved. But Arjun later asks, 'Did you help them prepare that argument?'

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The Follow-Up Check
rounds.situation: The Knowledge Festival happened, {player_name}. It was the school's biggest event this year — 400 attendees, combined science demos and creative writing workshops. Both clubs are being praised. The principal asks you: 'How did you get them to work together?' Before you answer, you notice Shruti and Arjun sitting together at lunch for the first time. The conflict is over. But is the peace built to last?
rounds.story: The mediator's final question isn't 'Did I solve the conflict?' but 'Can they handle the next one without me?'
rounds.image_prompt: Successful school Knowledge Festival with both clubs celebrating together, student mediator watching from the side with quiet satisfaction
rounds.coaching_moment: The best outcome of mediation isn't the agreement — it's two groups that learned how to talk to each other.
rounds.timer_narrative: The principal is waiting for your answer...

choices.label: Set up a regular check-in system
choices.description: Before stepping away, establish monthly joint meetings between both clubs. Teach them the mediation structure so they can facilitate themselves.
choices.consequence_hint: Builds long-term sustainability, but adds meetings that might not survive once the novelty fades

events.description: The monthly meetings become a tradition. The clubs co-plan three more events that year. Your structure outlasts your involvement.

choices.label: Let them fly — your job is done
choices.description: Trust that the relationship they've built will carry them. Step back completely. They don't need a mediator anymore.
choices.consequence_hint: Clean exit. Shows confidence in their growth. But if problems return, there's no safety net.

events.description: You see Shruti and Arjun disagreeing about something two months later. They resolve it themselves in 10 minutes. You smile.

choices.label: Train them as peer mediators
choices.description: Teach Shruti and Arjun the mediation skills you used. Let them become mediators for other school conflicts.
choices.consequence_hint: Multiplies the impact of your work, but requires time and commitment from students who already have full plates

events.description: Shruti and Arjun mediate a conflict between Class 7 and Class 8 the following month. They're better at it than they expected. The peace table continues.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

coaching_moment: Peace isn't the absence of conflict — it's the ability to handle conflict without destroying relationships.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: The Peace Table Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of The Peace Table. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
